blocks.text: The first rotor blades in a jet-engine compressor travel at about 250 m/s at mid-span, yet the air must meet each blade at a precise small angle or the flow separates and the engine can stall. Engineers check this by drawing a small triangle of three velocity vectors at every blade row. The triangle tells you the angle of attack, the work done and whether the machine is loaded sensibly.

blocks.markdown: In a rotating machine the fluid has two natural velocities. The **absolute velocity** $\vec c$ is what a stationary observer sees (a pitot probe, a stator vane). The **relative velocity** $\vec w$ is what an observer riding on the rotor sees; the blade surfaces are tangent to it. The blade moves at $\vec U$, so the three are related by vector addition.

blocks.title: The velocity triangle
blocks.text: At any station, $\vec c=\vec U+\vec w$. Draw $\vec U$ and $\vec w$ tip to tail and $\vec c$ closes the triangle. Components: axial $c_x$ (for axial machines; $c_r$ radial for radial machines) and whirl or tangential $c_\theta$ in the direction of $\vec U$. Angles are measured from the axial direction: $\alpha$ for $\vec c$ and $\beta$ for $\vec w$, in this lesson.

blocks.caption: Resolving the velocities (angles from the axial direction; whirl positive in the direction of rotation)

blocks.title: Triangles for an axial compressor rotor
blocks.prompt: Air enters a compressor rotor axially ($\alpha_1=0$) with $c_x=150$ m/s. Blade speed is $U=250$ m/s. The blades turn the relative flow so that it leaves at $\beta_2=45^\circ$ from the axial direction, against the direction of rotation, with $c_x$ unchanged. Find the relative inlet angle, the outlet absolute angle and the specific work.

steps.text: Inlet: with no absolute whirl, the relative velocity is just $-U$ in whirl plus the axial speed.
Outlet relative whirl, opposite to rotation.
Absolute whirl at outlet from $c_\theta=U+w_\theta$, then absolute angle and speed.
Euler work with zero inlet whirl.

rows: Sets the volume flow rate through the annulus
Direction of the blade surface at design
blocks.caption: Quantities obtained from a velocity triangle

blocks.markdown: **Non-dimensional coefficients.** Dividing flow and work by blade speed makes triangles comparable across machines. The **flow coefficient** $\phi=c_x/U$ measures how much through-flow there is per unit blade speed and the **blade loading (or work) coefficient** $\psi=\Delta h_0/U^2$ measures how much work is extracted per unit of $U^2$. Higher $\psi$ means more turning per stage; it is limited by diffusion and flow separation, with typical axial-compressor values of order 0.3 to 0.5 (typical).

blocks.title: A radial pump impeller outlet triangle
blocks.prompt: For this example the angle $\beta_2$ is measured from the tangent: a backward-swept impeller with $U_2=22$ m/s has radial velocity $c_r=4$ m/s and relative flow leaving at $\beta_2=30^\circ$ to the tangent, against the rotation. Resolve the absolute velocity.

steps.text: Relative whirl magnitude from the angle to the tangent.
Absolute whirl is blade speed minus this.
Absolute speed and angle from the radial direction.

items: Fix a sign convention for whirl (positive in the direction of $U$) and an angle reference (axial, here) before drawing.
Draw $\vec U$ first (known from speed and radius), then the known component of $\vec c$ or $\vec w$.
Use the blade angle for $\vec w$ and the stator or nozzle angle for $\vec c$, because that is the direction the flow follows at design.
Read $c_\theta$ and $c_x$ off the triangle; then apply Euler's equation for the work and compute $\phi$ and $\psi$.

blocks.title: Which components do what
blocks.text: The axial component carries the flow through the machine and fixes the mass flow rate; the whirl component carries the angular momentum that is exchanged with the blades. Doubling the whirl change at fixed blade speed doubles the work and doubles $\psi$, while changing the flow at fixed speed changes $\phi$ and moves the incidence of the relative flow on the blades.

points: Triangles obey $\vec c=\vec U+\vec w$; resolve into axial $c_x=c\cos\alpha$ and whirl $c_\theta=c\sin\alpha$ components.
Relative angles follow from $\tan\beta=w_\theta/c_x$; the relative flow follows the blade at design.
Flow coefficient $\phi=c_x/U$ and loading coefficient $\psi=\Delta h_0/U^2=\Delta c_\theta/U$ summarise a triangle.

questions.stem: The absolute velocity of the fluid leaving a nozzle row is 120 m/s at an angle of 60° from the axial direction. The whirl velocity and the axial velocity are respectively:

distractorRationale.a: Correct: whirl uses sine and axial uses cosine for angles from the axial direction.
distractorRationale.b: Swaps sine and cosine, which would be correct only for an angle measured from the tangential direction.
distractorRationale.c: Uses the tangent for whirl and takes the whole velocity as axial.
distractorRationale.d: Divides by the tangent, mixing up the ratio $c_\theta/c_x=\tan\alpha$.

questions.explanation: With the angle taken from the axial direction, $c_\theta=c\sin\alpha=120\sin60^\circ=103.9$ m/s and $c_x=c\cos\alpha=60$ m/s. The whirl is the larger component because the flow is steeply inclined.

questions.stem: Air enters a rotor with no absolute whirl, an axial velocity of 100 m/s and a blade speed of 200 m/s. The relative flow angle at the inlet, measured from the axial direction, is closest to:

distractorRationale.a: Uses $\tan\beta=c_x/U$, which gives the angle from the tangential direction.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: the angle from axial has tangent U over cx.
distractorRationale.c: Treats the relative flow as axial, which would need the blade to be stationary.
distractorRationale.d: Assumes equal axial and blade speeds, ignoring that $U$ is twice $c_x$.

questions.explanation: With no absolute whirl, the relative whirl is $-U$ so $\tan\beta_1=U/c_x=200/100=2$ and $\beta_1=63.43^\circ$ from the axial direction. The blades must be set close to this angle for the flow to enter smoothly.

questions.stem: A turbine stage has axial velocity 90 m/s and blade speed 300 m/s. Its flow coefficient $\phi=c_x/U$ is:

distractorRationale.b: Divides by an unrelated 1000 or the square of the speed.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: axial velocity divided by blade speed.
distractorRationale.d: Takes the axial velocity over 100 m/s, not the blade speed.

questions.explanation: The flow coefficient is $c_x/U=90/300=0.30$. It is a ratio of flow velocity to blade speed, so it is dimensionless and below one for most axial machines.

questions.stem: A compressor stage adds a stagnation enthalpy of 22.5 kJ/kg at a blade speed of 250 m/s. The loading coefficient $\psi=\Delta h_0/U^2$ is:

distractorRationale.b: Is off by a power of ten from mis-converting kJ to J.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: work in J/kg divided by the square of blade speed.

questions.explanation: $\psi=\Delta h_0/U^2=22\,500/62\,500=0.36$. Using work in J/kg and blade speed in m/s keeps the coefficient dimensionless.

questions.stem: An axial rotor takes in air with no whirl at fixed axial velocity. If the rotational speed is increased so that the blade speed rises, what happens to the relative inlet angle $\beta_1$ from the axial direction and to the flow coefficient?

options.text: Both are unchanged because the axial velocity is fixed

distractorRationale.a: Correct: both follow from tan beta equal to U over cx and phi equal to cx over U.
distractorRationale.b: Reverses both effects: a larger $U$ tilts the relative flow more tangentially.
distractorRationale.c: The angle trend is right but $\phi$ falls when its denominator $U$ rises.

questions.explanation: Since $\tan\beta_1=U/c_x$, a larger $U$ at fixed $c_x$ gives a larger angle from axial. The flow coefficient $c_x/U$ falls as its denominator rises, so the rotor operates at a lower $\phi$ and, for the same blade geometry, higher incidence.

questions.stem: Gas leaves a stator at 210 m/s at an angle of 40° from the axial direction. Find the whirl velocity component in m/s.
questions.explanation: The whirl component is $c_\theta=c\sin\alpha=210\sin40^\circ=135$ m/s, with the axial component $c\cos\alpha=160.9$ m/s.

questions.stem: Air enters a rotor axially at 110 m/s with blade speed 240 m/s. Construct the inlet triangle and find the magnitude of the relative velocity in m/s.
questions.explanation: The relative velocity is the vector sum of the axial velocity and the blade speed (reversed): $W_1=\sqrt{110^2+240^2}=264$ m/s. It exceeds both components, as the hypotenuse of the triangle.

questions.stem: A compressor stage takes air axially (no inlet whirl) with axial velocity 120 m/s and blade speed 280 m/s. The absolute flow leaves the rotor at 40° from the axial direction with unchanged axial velocity. Find the loading coefficient $\psi=\Delta c_\theta/U$ (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: The outlet whirl is $c_{\theta2}=c_x\tan40^\circ=100.7$ m/s, so the specific work is $Uc_{\theta2}=28194$ J/kg. Therefore $\psi=c_{\theta2}/U=100.7/280=0.3596$.

questions.stem: A fixed-geometry axial compressor rotor runs at constant speed. The throttle is closed so that the axial velocity falls. Using velocity triangles, explain what happens to the relative inlet angle, the flow coefficient and the loading coefficient, and why this can lead to blade stall.
markingGuide: Inlet triangle: with fixed U and falling cx, tan(beta1) = U/cx increases so relative flow angle from axial increases (more tangential)
Blade outlet relative angle is set by the blade geometry (and roughly unchanged), so the whirl change U - cx tan(beta2)-type expression rises as cx falls: work and loading psi increase
Incidence (difference between flow and blade angle) at the inlet increases
High incidence and higher loading increase diffusion and promote boundary-layer separation, so stall
Concludes that low flow coefficient combined with high loading is the stall-prone region
questions.explanation: At fixed blade speed, smaller $c_x$ raises $\tan\beta_1=U/c_x$, so the relative flow strikes the blade at greater incidence. The turning for fixed outlet blade angle yields larger $c_{\theta2}$ and so higher $\psi$, which adds diffusion in the passage and encourages separation.

questions.stem: Explain how an absolute velocity is resolved into whirl and axial components, and why the axial component determines the flow rate while the whirl component determines the work. Include a sketch description of the velocity triangle at the rotor outlet.
markingGuide: Defines c, U and w with c = U + w, drawn tip to tail
Resolves c into c_x = c cos(alpha) and c_theta = c sin(alpha) (angle from axial)
Mass flow = rho A c_x because only c_x crosses the annulus area
Euler work w = U (c_theta2 - c_theta1) depends only on whirl
Triangle description: U horizontal, c from the origin to the tip of w, with the angle alpha between c and the axial direction and beta between w and the axial direction
States that the relative velocity is parallel to the blade surface at design
questions.explanation: Only the axial component moves fluid through the flow area, so $\dot m=\rho A c_x$. The blades can exchange angular momentum only via the tangential component, so the work depends on the whirl change alone.
